topics.title: “Terrorists” Under UAPA
bullets: On 4 July 2026, the Union Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) designated 23 individuals as "terrorists" under Section 35 of the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA), 1967.
Of the 23 designated, 17 are Pakistani nationals and six are Indian nationals, all of whom are alleged to be operating from Pakistan and Pakistan-occupied Kashmir (PoK).
With this latest notification, the total number of individuals designated as terrorists under the UAPA now stands at 80. What is the UAPA? –
The UAPA is India's primary anti-terrorism law, enacted to provide for the more effective prevention of certain unlawful activities of individuals and associations.
It was enacted in the aftermath of the 1962 war with China and the 1965 war with Pakistan, when the government felt the need to strengthen internal security.
The Act received the assent of the President on 30 December 1967.
Initially, the UAPA was designed to curb activities prejudicial to national integration.
Over time, it was transformed into a harsh anti-terrorist law, especially after the 2004 amendments inserted a dedicated chapter on terrorist activities.
The 2004 amendments were introduced to overcome difficulties in enforcement and to update the law in accordance with international commitments.
In August 2019, the UAPA was amended to include a provision for designating an individual as a terrorist.
Prior to this amendment, only organizations could be designated as terrorist organizations.
The amendment empowered the government to designate individuals as terrorists regardless of whether they were members of a banned organization.
Designating individuals as terrorists allows agencies such as the National Investigation Agency (NIA) to block their finances, impose an embargo on arms sales, and seize their assets.
It also enables the government to track and monitor the activities of these individuals more effectively.
This provision was introduced because previously, when terrorist organizations were banned, the individuals associated with them would simply change names and continue their activities.
The Fourth Schedule of the UAPA contains the list of individuals designated as terrorists.
Once an individual's name is added to the Fourth Schedule, they are officially recognized as a "terrorist" under Indian law.
The total number of individuals in this schedule now stands at 80.
Following the 2019 amendment, the government designated the first four individuals as terrorists.
They were: Masood Azhar (Jaish-e-Mohammed chief), Hafiz Saeed (Lashkar-e-Taiba founder), Zaki-ur-Rehman Lakhvi (Mumbai attack accused), and Dawood Ibrahim (fugitive gangster).
These designations were made through a gazette notification on 4 September 2019.
The 2019 amendment also allowed for the designation of "extremists" and "insurgents" as terrorists if the government had "sufficient proof".
This expanded the scope of the law beyond traditional terrorist organizations.
The amendment was passed by Parliament in August 2019. Recent News –
The MHA designated 23 Pakistan-based individuals linked to Jaish-e-Mohammed (JeM) and Lashkar-e-Taiba (LeT) as terrorists.
The list includes close aides of LeT founder Hafiz Saeed and key functionaries of JeM.
Among those designated are Hafiz Khalid Walid (son-in-law of Hafiz Saeed and mastermind of the 2016 Pampore attack) and Masood Ilyas Kashmiri (a close confidant of JeM chief Maulana Masood Azhar).
The designated individuals are involved in anti-India activities, including carrying out terror attacks, inciting terror, trafficking arms, and infiltrating through the border.
They are also accused of recruiting terrorists, raising funds, and facilitating terrorist organisations.
Some of the individuals were involved in reconnaissance of sites like the Ram Mandir complex and the RSS headquarters.

The designated individuals have been linked to several major terror attacks, including: ➢Pathankot air base attack (2016) ➢Pampore attack (2016) – in which eight CRPF personnel were killed ➢Nagrota attack (2016) ➢Sunjuwan attack (2022) ➢Rameshwaram Cafe blast (2024)
Among the six Indians designated is Mohammed Shaheed, a Bengaluru native currently based in Rawalpindi. He is accused of recruiting youth via social media for terror activities.
All six Indians are alleged to be operating from Pakistan and PoK.
One of the individuals, Maulana Imdad Ullakh Makki, was involved in real-time coordination with terrorists who struck at the Pathankot air base.
Once designated, the individual's assets can be frozen and seized.
They become subject to travel bans and other restrictions.
Designation also enables law enforcement agencies to monitor their activities more closely.
The UAPA provides for special procedures to decide cases with respect to terrorism, given the heinous nature of the crime.
Section 43E of the UAPA alters the foundational principle of criminal law by placing a reverse burden of proof on the accused in terrorist act prosecutions.
This means that the accused is presumed guilty until proven innocent, a significant departure from standard criminal law.
Critics argue that clauses such as Section 35(2) give the government a free hand in designating any individual as a terrorist, which could be used to detain political opponents.
The reverse burden of proof provision has also been challenged on constitutional grounds.
The constitutionality of the UAPA amendments has been challenged in the Supreme Court.
The UAPA has been used to designate individuals as terrorists, demonstrating the government's commitment to combating terrorism.
The law has been strengthened over the years, especially after the 26/11 Mumbai terror attacks (2008), to address emerging threats.
The UAPA remains a key tool for India's internal security apparatus.

topics.title: Gwadar Port Attack
bullets: The Pakistan Coast Guard camp outside Jiwani in Gwadar was rocked by a suicide truck bombing on 3 July 2026, with the Baloch Liberation Army (BLA) claiming over 30 security personnel were killed.
Gwadar, a remote town with a population of under 100,000, sits on a strategic chessboard – a few hundred kilometres from the Strait of Hormuz, a critical route for global oil shipments.

The port is the maritime end of the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC), making it a prime target for Baloch separatists who see the project as exploitation of their resources without local benefits. Background –
Balochistan is Pakistan's largest province by area, rich in natural resources including natural gas, copper, and gold, but remains Pakistan's poorest and least developed region.
The province has a distinct ethnic identity and has been suffering from insurgency since the late 1950s.
Its coastline along the Arabian Sea, including Gwadar, has become a focal point of geopolitical rivalry between China, Pakistan, and India.
The roots of the Baloch insurgency trace back to the contested annexation of the princely state of Kalat in 1948, months after the partition of British India.
On 27 March 1948, Pakistan forcibly annexed Balochistan – a move widely viewed by the Baloch as illegitimate.
This annexation created a foundational grievance that has fueled separatist sentiment for over seven decades.
Pakistan's "One Unit" scheme, which dissolved provincial identities in West Pakistan into a single administrative unit in 1955, triggered the second major Baloch uprising in 1958.
The scheme was seen as an attempt to erase Baloch identity and political autonomy.
This uprising marked the beginning of decades of violent resistance and military crackdowns.
Inspired by the secession of East Pakistan in 1971, Baloch rebels fought for nearly four years (1973-1977) before being crushed by superior military force.
The insurgency was led by Nawab Akbar Khan Bugti and other Baloch tribal leaders.
The rebellion resulted in thousands of deaths and deepened the mistrust between the Baloch people and the Pakistani state.
The Baloch Liberation Army (BLA) is the most prominent Baloch separatist militant group fighting for an independent Balochistan.

The group has claimed responsibility for multiple attacks, including the 2024 suicide bombings near Karachi airport and Gwadar port, and the 2025 hijacking of the Jaffar Express train, which killed 31 and held over 300 hostage.
In August 2025, the US designated the BLA as a "terror group".
Many analysts and Baloch people themselves say the roots of the insurgency are local: political neglect, weak institutions, and a failure to share the region's wealth.
The Baloch have historically been excluded from decision- making, with power concentrated in Islamabad and Rawalpindi.
Enforced disappearances, extrajudicial killings, and human rights abuses have also fueled the insurgency. What is Gwadar Port? –
Gwadar is a deep-sea port on the southwestern coast of Balochistan, Pakistan, located near the Strait of Hormuz.
The port was developed by China under the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC).
For Beijing, Gwadar promises a shorter, alternative route for goods and energy, bypassing the Strait of Malacca.
Launched in 2013, CPEC is a $62 billion infrastructure project connecting Pakistan's southwest Gwadar port with Kashgar in Northwest China's Xinjiang region.
It is a flagship project of China's Belt and Road Initiative (BRI).
CPEC includes energy, transport, and industrial cooperation, with a focus on creating a regional trade and logistics hub.
CPEC has now entered a more complex second phase that emphasizes industrialization, technology, agriculture, Special Economic Zones (SEZs), and digital connectivity.
Gwadar is emerging as the "strategic heart" of CPEC, with a concentration of petrochemical, agricultural, logistics, and industrial projects.
Pakistan aims to use Gwadar as a hub for the mining industry, linking its mineral resources with global markets.
Gwadar offers China additional connectivity to the Indian Ocean, helping diversify China's shipping channels beyond the Strait of Malacca.
It provides a shorter, alternative route for goods and energy from the Middle East to China.
The port also gives China a strategic foothold in the Arabian Sea, near critical oil shipping lanes.
Pakistan sees Gwadar as a long-awaited chance to boost trade and build a stronger naval presence on its southwest coast.
The port is expected to transform Pakistan from a traditional consumer economy into a regional transit and logistics hub.
CPEC is projected to bring significant economic dividends for future generations.
Pakistan built a $240 million airport in Gwadar, but it stands largely idle with no flights and no passengers.
The government claims CPEC has created 2,000 local jobs, but it is unclear whether "local" means Baloch residents or workers from other provinces.
This has become a symbol of unfulfilled promises and a source of local frustration.
Residents of Gwadar held 47 days of demonstrations before authorities promised to address local concerns, including improved access to water and electricity.
The protests highlighted the deep-seated grievances of the local population.
This shows that the discontent is not just about security but about basic needs and dignity. Recent News –

On 3 July 2026, at around 6:32 PM, a suicide commando (fidayee) from the BLA's Majeed Brigade drove an explosives- laden vehicle into a Pakistan Coast Guard camp in the Panwan area of Jiwani, Gwadar, and detonated it.
The attack involved a suicide truck bombing and a ground assault on the fortified Coast Guard camp.
The BLA claimed over 30 security personnel were killed and dozens wounded, though official casualty figures were unclear at the time of reporting.
The BLA used a vehicle-borne improvised explosive device (SVBIED) – a truck bomb.
The BLA's Majeed Brigade – a unit known for complex operations – carried out the assault.
This indicates a shift from roadside bombs to more sophisticated, targeted attacks on fortified positions.
Attacks used to mean roadside bombs or ambushes. Now militants carry out more complex operations – targeting port facilities, naval outposts, patrol boats, and even using drones.
The BLA has formed wings that operate at sea and in the air, showing they are trying to widen the battlefield beyond classic guerrilla tactics.
Friday's assault shows that the threat remains adaptive and deadly.
Islamabad created a dedicated security division to protect Chinese workers and strategic projects.
Security around Gwadar was tightened after earlier incidents.
Still, militants keep finding new targets, indicating that the security measures are not fully effective.
China has invested billions of dollars in Gwadar and CPEC.
The attacks on Chinese engineers and projects in Gwadar have prompted an intensified crackdown on separatists, straining Pakistan-China relations further.
Beijing's national security concerns are now directly linked to the stability of Balochistan. Belt and Road Initiative –
BRI was launched by Xi Jinping in 2013 to enhance connectivity through infrastructure, trade, investment and people-to-people exchanges across Asia, Europe, Africa and beyond.
It comprises two components: the Silk Road Economic Belt (land corridors) and the 21st Century Maritime Silk Road (sea routes).
The BRI is China's flagship global infrastructure initiative and now involves around 150 participating countries and international organisations through cooperation agreements.
Critics have raised concerns regarding debt sustainability, lack of transparency, environmental impact and China's growing geopolitical influence through infrastructure financing.
India has not joined the BRI, primarily because the China– Pakistan Economic Corridor passes through Pakistan-occupied Kashmir, which India considers its sovereign territory.
In recent years, China has shifted the BRI towards smaller, high- quality and more sustainable projects, focusing on financial sustainability and technology-driven connectivity
